title: X-Ray Diffraction
short_intro: X-ray diffraction is the elastic scattering of X-ray photons by the regularly spaced atoms of a crystalline lattice, resulting in constructive interference when Bragg's condition is satisfied. It serves as a primary experimental tool for determining crystal structures and interatomic spacings.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Bragg's Law formulation (2d sin(θ) = nλ), condition for constructive interference, and basic identification of crystal planes from numerical problems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of reciprocal lattice relation, structure factor calculations, Laue equations, and systematic absences for different cubic lattices (SC, BCC, FCC).

concept_notes.heading: Bragg's Law of X-Ray Diffraction
bullets: When an X-ray beam strikes a crystal plane at a glancing angle θ, the path difference between rays reflected from adjacent planes separated by interplanar spacing d is given by 2d sin(θ).
Constructive interference occurs when this path difference is an integral multiple of the X-ray wavelength λ.
The intensity of the diffracted beam reaches a maximum only when Bragg's condition 2d sin(θ) = nλ is strictly satisfied.

concept_notes.heading: Reciprocal Lattice and Ewald Sphere
bullets: The reciprocal lattice is a mathematical construct in Fourier space where each point corresponds to a specific set of parallel planes (hkl) in the real crystal lattice.
The position vector of a reciprocal lattice point has a magnitude inversely proportional to the interplanar spacing d<sub>hkl</sub>.

The Ewald sphere construction provides a geometric interpretation of Bragg's law, where diffraction occurs if and only if a reciprocal lattice point intersects the surface of the sphere of radius 1/λ.

concept_notes.heading: Atomic Scattering Factor and Structure Factor
bullets: The atomic scattering factor (f) measures the efficiency of wave scattering by a single atom, depending on the atomic number Z and the diffraction angle θ.
The geometric structure factor (F<sub>hkl</sub>) accounts for the phase differences of waves scattered by different atoms within the same unit cell.
Systematic absences in F<sub>hkl</sub> values allow identification of centering types in Bravais lattices, such as missing (h+k+l) odd for BCC structures.

concept_notes.heading: Experimental Methods in X-Ray Diffraction
bullets: The Laue method uses a stationary single crystal and a continuous (polychromatic) beam of X-rays to obtain diffraction patterns showing crystal symmetry.
The rotating crystal method employs a monochromatic X-ray beam on a rotating single crystal to map out multiple lattice planes.
The powder (Debye-Scherrer) method uses a finely powdered polycrystalline sample, producing continuous cones of diffraction corresponding to all possible sets of lattice planes.

derivations.title: Derivation of Bragg's Law
derivations.conditions: Parallel monochromatic X-ray beams incident on parallel crystal planes separated by distance d at glancing angle θ.
steps: Consider two parallel incident rays falling on successive atomic planes separated by interplanar distance d at a glancing angle θ.
Draw perpendiculars from the point of reflection of the first ray to the incident and reflected paths of the second ray to determine the path difference.
The path difference for the second ray relative to the first is given by the geometric sum of segments: Δ = d sin(θ) + d sin(θ) = 2d sin(θ).
For constructive interference to occur, this path difference must equal an integer multiple of the wavelength λ.

derivations.title: Interplanar Spacing for Cubic Systems
derivations.conditions: Orthogonal crystal system with lattice parameter a and Miller indices (hkl).
steps: The general formula for interplanar spacing d in an orthogonal system is expressed in terms of reciprocal metric tensor components.
For a cubic crystal system, the axial lengths are equal: a = b = c and interaxial angles are 90 degrees (α = β = γ = 90 degrees).
Substitute the cubic conditions into the interplanar spacing formula: 1 / d^{2} = h^{2}/a^{2} + k^{2}/a^{2} + l^{2}/a^{2}.
Factor out 1/a^{2} and take the square root of both sides to obtain d.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Debye-Scherrer Powder Diffraction Pattern
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A strip diagram or photographic film showing distinct, curved vertical arc lines corresponding to different (hkl) reflections at various angles 2θ.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Each arc represents constructive interference from a specific set of lattice planes in randomly oriented microcrystals.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to test identification of crystal structures (SC, BCC, FCC) from line positions and indexing ratios.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Intensity vs 2θ Diffractogram
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of X-ray intensity (counts/sec) on the y-axis against 2θ (degrees) on the x-axis, showing sharp peaks at specific angles.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Sharp peaks indicate long-range crystalline order, and peak positions directly yield interplanar spacings via Bragg's law.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting phase purity, lattice parameters, and crystallite size using the Scherrer formula.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Ewald Sphere Construction
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A sphere of radius 1/λ in reciprocal space passing through the origin, with a set of reciprocal lattice points around it.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Diffraction occurs exclusively when a reciprocal lattice point lies precisely on the surface of the Ewald sphere.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Explaining geometric conditions for diffraction and reciprocal space mapping.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the interplanar spacing of a crystal plane that gives the first-order diffraction maximum at a Bragg angle of 30 degrees for X-rays of wavelength 1.5 Å.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: n = 1, θ = 30 degrees, λ = 1.5 Å = 1.5 × 10^{-10} m.
Since sin(30 degrees) = 0.5, 2 d (0.5) = 1.5 × 10^{-10} gives d = 1.5 × 10^{-10} m.

solved_numericals.question: A cubic crystal has a lattice parameter a = 3.0 Å. Determine the Bragg angle for the (110) planes in the first-order diffraction using monochromatic X-rays of wavelength 1.0 Å.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: a = 3.0 Å, h = 1, k = 1, l = 0, n = 1, λ = 1.0 Å.
Calculate interplanar spacing d for cubic system: d = a / \sqrt{h^{2} + k^{2} + l^{2}}.

solved_numericals.question: In an X-ray diffraction powder pattern using copper K-alpha radiation (λ = 1.54 Å), lines are observed for a face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal. If the lattice constant a = 4.0 Å, find the glancing angle for the (200) planes with n = 1.
solution_steps: Identify parameters: a = 4.0 Å, h = 2, k = 0, l = 0, λ = 1.54 Å, n = 1.
Calculate interplanar spacing d for (200): d = 4.0 / \sqrt{2^{2} + 0^{2} + 0^{2}} = 4.0 / 2 = 2.0 Å.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes the crystal is perfectly ordered and infinite, which neglects finite-size broadening effects.
Assumes kinematic diffraction theory (single scattering), ignoring dynamical diffraction effects where multiple scattering occurs in large perfect crystals.
Wavelength of incident X-rays must be comparable to the interplanar spacing (typically 0.5 Å to 2.5 Å) for diffraction to be observable.

common_misconceptions.wrong: X-rays are reflected from the front surface of the crystal like a mirror.
common_misconceptions.correct: X-rays penetrate deep into the crystal and are scattered by electrons surrounding lattice atoms across multiple parallel planes.
common_misconceptions.why: Reflection implies surface interaction, whereas diffraction is a volumetric scattering and interference phenomenon.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Bragg angle θ is measured between the incident ray and the crystal surface.
common_misconceptions.correct: The glancing angle θ is measured between the incident X-ray beam and the crystal lattice planes (not the physical surface, unless planes are parallel to the surface).
common_misconceptions.why: Misinterpreting the reference plane leads to incorrect path difference calculations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Any wavelength of X-rays can produce diffraction from any set of crystal planes.
common_misconceptions.correct: Diffraction occurs only when λ ≤ 2d, since sin(θ) cannot exceed unity.
common_misconceptions.why: Mathematical constraint imposed by the sine function in Bragg's law.

quick_revision: Bragg's Law: 2d sin(θ) = nλ is the fundamental condition for constructive interference of X-rays in crystals.
Cubic Interplanar Spacing: d_{hkl} = \frac{a}{\sqrt{h^{2} + k^{2} + l^{2}}}
